questions.stem: Panel B of this diagram shows a congenital variant in which the dorsal and ventral pancreatic ducts fail to fuse, so most exocrine secretions drain through the minor papilla. What is the principal clinical consequence of this anatomy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obstructive jaundice from common bile duct compression

choices.label: D
choices.text: Duodenal obstruction from an encircling pancreatic ring

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impaired drainage predisposing to recurrent pancreatitis

explanation.summary: Failure of dorsal and ventral duct fusion routes most pancreatic juice through the small minor papilla; the relative outflow resistance can raise ductal pressure and predispose to recurrent acute or chronic pancreatitis, though most cases are asymptomatic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Failure of dorsal and ventral duct fusion routes most pancreatic juice through the small minor papilla; the relative outflow resistance can raise ductal pressure and predispose to recurrent acute or chronic pancreatitis, though most cases are asymptomatic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreas divisum preserves functioning acinar tissue and drains enzymes through the minor papilla, so it does not cause exocrine insufficiency from birth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Common bile duct compression causing jaundice is typical of a pancreatic head mass or annular pancreas, not of unfused ducts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biliary atresia is obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts in infancy and is unrelated to pancreatic duct fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An encircling ring of pancreatic tissue around the duodenum is annular pancreas, a different anomaly of ventral bud rotation.

questions.stem: These CT and plain abdominal film images show scattered radiodensities distributed throughout the pancreatic parenchyma. This finding is considered virtually pathognomonic for which condition?

explanation.summary: Parenchymal calcifications are the most reliable imaging finding of established chronic pancreatitis, reflecting calcified intraductal protein plugs; they are nearly 100% specific and are most common in advanced alcohol-related disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Parenchymal calcifications are the most reliable imaging finding of established chronic pancreatitis, reflecting calcified intraductal protein plugs; they are nearly 100% specific and are most common in advanced alcohol-related disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pseudocyst is a fluid collection with a fibrous wall, appearing as a low-density cyst rather than scattered calcifications.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute interstitial pancreatitis causes an enlarged, edematous pancreas with peripancreatic stranding, not parenchymal calcification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ductal adenocarcinoma is a hypoenhancing mass that may obstruct ducts; calcification is uncommon and not pathognomonic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gallstone ileus shows pneumobilia, small bowel obstruction, and an ectopic gallstone (Rigler triad), not pancreatic calcifications.

questions.stem: This schematic illustrates the sequential activation of a pancreatic cell type during chronic injury. According to this pathway, the irreversible fibrosis of chronic pancreatitis results primarily from which process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transformation of stellate cells into myofibroblast-like cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ischemic coagulative necrosis from vascular thrombosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutrophil-mediated proteolytic digestion of the parenchyma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regenerative hyperplasia of ductal epithelial cells

explanation.summary: Recurrent injury activates normally quiescent, vitamin A-storing pancreatic stellate cells, which lose their lipid droplets and transform into myofibroblast-like cells that deposit collagen and extracellular matrix, driving progressive fibrosis and ductal narrowing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent injury activates normally quiescent, vitamin A-storing pancreatic stellate cells, which lose their lipid droplets and transform into myofibroblast-like cells that deposit collagen and extracellular matrix, driving progressive fibrosis and ductal narrowing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ischemic coagulative necrosis is not the main mechanism of chronic pancreatitis, and dead tissue is replaced by matrix laid down by activated cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophil-mediated proteolysis and enzyme autodigestion drive acute pancreatitis, not the progressive collagen deposition of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ductal epithelial hyperplasia does not produce the collagen that causes fibrosis; ducts are instead narrowed and distorted by it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Islet amyloid is characteristic of type 2 diabetes, not the fibrotic replacement of the exocrine parenchyma in chronic pancreatitis.

questions.stem: This contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with a pancreatic head mass shows simultaneous dilation of both the main pancreatic duct and the common bile duct (arrows). This radiologic finding is known as what?

explanation.summary: A mass in the pancreatic head can simultaneously obstruct the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct, dilating both. This 'double-duct sign' is highly suggestive of pancreatic head carcinoma. The double-bubble sign refers to duodenal atresia, and the colon cutoff/sentinel loop signs are seen in pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A mass in the pancreatic head can simultaneously obstruct the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct, dilating both. This 'double-duct sign' is highly suggestive of pancreatic head carcinoma. The double-bubble sign refers to duodenal atresia, and the colon cutoff/sentinel loop signs are seen in pancreatitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The sentinel loop sign is a single dilated jejunal loop near an inflamed pancreas in acute pancreatitis, not dilation of two ducts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The double-bubble sign is gas in a distended stomach and duodenum from duodenal atresia or annular pancreas in neonates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Courvoisier sign is a palpable, nontender gallbladder with jaundice, a physical exam finding rather than a CT finding of two dilated ducts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The colon cutoff sign is abrupt loss of gas at the splenic flexure from adjacent pancreatic inflammation in acute pancreatitis.

questions.stem: This schematic depicts the pathway activated when a cell detects DNA damage: it halts the cell cycle to permit repair, or, if damage is too severe, drives the cell toward programmed cell death. The gene encoding the central protein shown is inactivated in roughly 50-75% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas. On which chromosome is that gene located?

explanation.summary: The pathway shown centers on p53, the tumor-suppressor 'guardian of the genome,' which is encoded by TP53 on chromosome 17p. p53 halts the cell cycle for DNA repair or triggers apoptosis; its inactivation is a late-stage event in ~50-75% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas. KRAS is on 12p, p16/CDKN2A on 9p, and DPC4/SMAD4 on 18q.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pathway shown centers on p53, the tumor-suppressor 'guardian of the genome,' which is encoded by TP53 on chromosome 17p. p53 halts the cell cycle for DNA repair or triggers apoptosis; its inactivation is a late-stage event in ~50-75% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas. KRAS is on 12p, p16/CDKN2A on 9p, and DPC4/SMAD4 on 18q.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromosome 9p carries CDKN2A (p16), a G1 cell-cycle inhibitor lost in most pancreatic cancers, not the DNA-damage guardian shown.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromosome 18q carries SMAD4 (DPC4), a TGF-beta pathway gene lost in about half of pancreatic cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosome 12p carries KRAS, an oncogene activated early in nearly all pancreatic cancers, not a tumor suppressor that triggers apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chromosome 11q carries ATM, a DNA-damage kinase upstream of the central protein, and MEN1, but not the gene in question.
